These three steps give the developer a clear picture of their resource usage before
committing to an API call. In the VS Code extension, this information is always visible in
the sidebar without needing to type any commands.


\section{Related Tools}

Several token counting utilities exist as standalone web pages or CLI scripts.
\texttt{tiktoken}~\cite{tiktoken} is the reference OpenAI tokenizer library.
Anthropic provides a tokenizer SDK for Claude models. Tokalator differs from these in three
ways: it integrates directly into the development environment rather than requiring a
separate tool, it scores file relevance rather than only counting tokens, and it connects
token counts to dollar costs using current provider pricing.


\section{Availability}

Tokalator is open source under the MIT license. The VS Code extension is published on the
Visual Studio Marketplace. The MCP server can be installed from npm. The web platform is
deployed on Vercel. All source code is available at
\url{https://github.com/vfaraji89/tokalator}.

content.text:
The paper compiles cleanly to 3 pages. Here is what it covers:

- **Abstract**: One paragraph summary of what Tokalator does and its three components.
- **Section 1 (Introduction)**: The problem (developers cannot see token usage or costs), and how Tokalator solves it with live counts, relevance scores, and cost estimates.
- **Section 2 (System Architecture)**: Three subsections covering the VS Code extension (real-time sidebar, chat participant, real tokenizers), the MCP server (4 tools over stdio), and the web platform (calculators, Cobb-Douglas analysis).
- **Section 3 (Relevance Scoring)**: The weighted linear formula $R = w_l S_l + w_i S_i + w_p S_p + w_r S_r + w_d S_d$ with a table of the five signals and their weights.
- **Section 4 (Cost Model)**: The token cost equation and the Cobb-Douglas quality function.
- **Section 5 (Usage Example)**: Three concrete steps (count tokens, estimate budget, preview turn) with formatted output.
- **Section 6 (Related Tools and Availability)**: Comparison with tiktoken and Anthropic SDK, plus links.

The file is at `paper/demo-paper.tex` and the compiled PDF is at `paper/demo-paper.pdf`.

22	  basicstyle=\small\ttfamily\color{codetext},

32	\title{Tokalator: A Token Budget Monitor and Cost Estimator\\for AI-Assisted Software Development}
33	
34	\author{
35	  Vahid Faraji \\
36	  \texttt{vfaraji89@gmail.com}
37	}
38	
39	\date{}
40	
41	\begin{document}
42	\maketitle
43	
44	\begin{abstract}
45	Large language models used in code editors process context through fixed-size token windows.
46	Developers who use AI assistants such as GitHub Copilot or Claude Code often have no
47	visibility into how much of that window their open files, instructions, and conversation
48	history consume. Tokalator is an open-source toolkit that makes token usage visible and
49	actionable. It consists of three components: a VS Code extension with a real-time sidebar
50	dashboard, an MCP server that brings token counting into Claude Code, and a web platform
51	with cost calculators and economic analysis tools. This paper describes the system
52	architecture, the relevance scoring algorithm, and the cost model. We show a step-by-step
53	usage example and discuss how the tool helps developers reduce unnecessary spending on
54	AI API calls.
55	\end{abstract}
56	
57	
58	\section{Introduction}
59	
60	When a developer asks an AI coding assistant to fix a bug or write a function, the assistant
61	reads the open files, the conversation history, and any attached instructions. All of this
62	text is converted into tokens before the model processes it. Each model has a maximum number
63	of tokens it can handle at once, called the context window. For example, Claude Opus 4.6
64	has a context window of 200,000 tokens.
65	
66	The problem is that developers cannot see how many tokens their current session uses. A
67	developer with 30 open tabs may not realize that those files alone consume 60\% of the
68	context window, leaving little room for the model to produce a useful response. Worse, every
69	token sent to the API has a dollar cost. Teams that run hundreds of AI-assisted sessions per
70	day can accumulate significant bills without understanding where the money goes.
71	
72	Tokalator solves this problem. The name combines ``token'' and ``calculator,'' inspired by the
73	abacus as a simple counting tool. It gives developers three things: (1) a live count of how
74	many tokens their current editor state uses, (2) a relevance score for each open file so they
75	know which tabs matter and which waste budget, and (3) a cost estimate based on current
76	provider pricing.
77	
78	
79	\section{System Architecture}
80	
81	Tokalator has three independent components that share a common core logic.
82	
83	\subsection{VS Code Extension}
84	
85	The extension adds a sidebar panel to VS Code that updates in real time. When a developer
86	opens, closes, or edits a file, the extension recalculates the token count and the budget
87	breakdown. It also provides a chat participant (\texttt{@tokalator}) that responds to
88	commands such as \texttt{/count}, \texttt{/breakdown}, and \texttt{/optimize}.
89	
90	The extension uses the real Claude BPE tokenizer from the Anthropic SDK for Claude models
91	and the \texttt{o200k\_base} tokenizer from \texttt{js-tiktoken} for OpenAI models. For
92	Google models, it applies a heuristic of approximately one token per four characters.
93	
94	\subsection{MCP Server}
95	
96	The Model Context Protocol (MCP) server exposes four tools over stdio JSON-RPC:
97	\texttt{count\_tokens}, \texttt{estimate\_budget}, \texttt{preview\_turn}, and
98	\texttt{list\_models}. When registered in the \texttt{.mcp.json} configuration file, Claude
99	Code loads these tools automatically. A developer can then ask Claude Code to count tokens
100	or estimate the budget without leaving the terminal.
101	
102	\subsection{Web Platform}
103	
104	The web application, built with Next.js, provides interactive calculators for token cost
105	estimation, caching ROI analysis, and model comparison. It also hosts an economic analysis
106	tool based on the Cobb-Douglas quality function from Bergemann, Bonatti, and
107	Smolin~\cite{bergemann2025}.
108	
109	
110	\section{Relevance Scoring}
111	
112	Not all open files are equally useful to the AI assistant. Tokalator assigns each open tab a
113	relevance score $R \in [0, 1]$ using five weighted signals:
114	
115	\begin{equation}
116	R = w_l \cdot S_l + w_i \cdot S_i + w_p \cdot S_p + w_r \cdot S_r + w_d \cdot S_d
117	\end{equation}
118	
119	\noindent where the signals and their default weights are:
120	
121	\begin{table}[H]
122	\centering
123	\small
124	\begin{tabular}{@{}llp{5.5cm}@{}}
125	\toprule
126	Signal & Weight & Description \\
127	\midrule
128	Language match ($S_l$)  & 0.25 & 1 if the tab shares the same programming language as the active file, 0 otherwise \\
129	Import relation ($S_i$) & 0.30 & 1 if the active file imports or requires the tab file \\
130	Path similarity ($S_p$) & 0.20 & Ratio of shared directory prefix segments to total depth \\
131	Edit recency ($S_r$)    & 0.15 & 1 if edited within the last 2 minutes, decays over time \\
132	Diagnostics ($S_d$)     & 0.10 & 1 if the tab has compiler errors or warnings \\
133	\bottomrule
134	\end{tabular}
135	\caption{Relevance scoring signals and default weights.}
136	\label{tab:weights}
137	\end{table}
138

}

\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
AI coding assistants read your open files, conversation history, and instructions before
they generate a response. All of this text is broken into tokens, and every model has a
limit on how many tokens it can process at once. Developers today have no easy way to
see how much of that limit they are using or how much it costs. Tokalator is an
open-source toolkit that shows you this information in real time. It has three parts: a
VS Code extension with a live dashboard, an MCP server that works inside Claude Code,
and a web platform with cost calculators. This paper explains what Tokalator is, how to
install each part, and how to use it in everyday development work.
\end{abstract}


\section{What Is Tokalator}

When you ask an AI assistant to write code or fix a bug, it does not just read your
question. It also reads the files you have open, any instruction files in your project,
and the full conversation you have had so far. The assistant converts all of this text
into small pieces called tokens. A single English word is usually one or two tokens. A
line of code might be five to ten tokens.

Every AI model has a maximum number of tokens it can handle at once. This is called the
context window. Claude Opus 4.6, for example, can handle 200,000 tokens at a time. If
your open files and conversation history use up most of that window, the model has less
room to think and produce a good answer.

On top of that, tokens cost money. Providers like Anthropic and OpenAI charge per million
tokens. If you send 50,000 input tokens to Claude Sonnet 4.5, that single request costs
about \$0.15. Over hundreds of requests per day, the cost adds up.

Tokalator makes these numbers visible. The name comes from ``token'' and ``calculator.''
It works like an abacus for your AI usage: it counts what goes in, shows you what each
piece costs, and tells you which files are actually useful to the assistant and which ones
are wasting space.


\section{The Three Components}

Tokalator has three parts. You can use any of them on their own or together.

\textbf{VS Code Extension.} A sidebar panel inside VS Code that shows a live token count,
a budget bar, and a relevance score for each open tab. It also adds a chat participant
called \texttt{@tokalator} that you can talk to inside VS Code Chat.

\textbf{MCP Server.} A small server that runs in the background and gives Claude Code
access to four tools: count tokens, estimate your budget, preview the cost of your next
message, and list available models. Claude Code loads it automatically from the project
configuration.

\textbf{Web Platform.} A website with interactive calculators where you can compare model
prices, estimate caching savings, and analyze costs for different usage patterns.


\section{How to Install}

\subsection{Installing the VS Code Extension}

Open VS Code and go to the Extensions panel. Search for ``Tokalator'' and click Install.
You can also install it from the terminal:

\begin{lstlisting}
code --install-extension vfaraji89.tokalator
\end{lstlisting}

After installation, a new icon appears in the Activity Bar on the left side of VS Code.
Click it to open the Tokalator sidebar.

\subsection{Setting Up the MCP Server}

The MCP server lets Claude Code use Tokalator tools directly in the terminal. To set it
up, add the following to the \texttt{.mcp.json} file in your project root:

\begin{lstlisting}
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "tokalator": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "tokalator-mcp@latest"]
    }
  }
}
\end{lstlisting}

The next time you start Claude Code in that project, it will load the Tokalator tools
automatically. You do not need to run any extra commands.

\subsection{Using the Web Platform}

Visit the Tokalator website to use the online calculators. No installation is needed.
The site includes a token cost calculator, a caching ROI estimator, a model comparison
table, and a conversation budget planner.


\section{How to Use the VS Code Extension}

Once installed, the extension starts working right away. Here is what you can do with it.

\subsection{Reading the Sidebar Dashboard}

The sidebar shows three things at a glance:

\begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item \textbf{Budget bar.} A progress bar that fills up as you use more tokens. It
    shows how much of the model's context window you have used. Green means comfortable,
    yellow means you are getting close to the limit, and red means you are near full.
  \item \textbf{Token breakdown.} A list that shows where your tokens are going: open
    files, system prompt, instruction files, conversation history, and output reservation.
  \item \textbf{Tab list with scores.} Every open tab appears with its token count and a
    relevance score from 0 to 1. A score near 1 means the file is important to the
    assistant. A score near 0 means it is probably not needed.
\end{itemize}

The dashboard updates every time you open, close, or edit a file. You do not need to
refresh anything.

\subsection{Using Chat Commands}

Type \texttt{@tokalator} in VS Code Chat followed by a command. Here are the most useful
ones:

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lp{7.5cm}@{}}
\toprule
Command & What it does \\
\midrule
\texttt{/count} & Shows the total token count and budget status \\
\texttt{/breakdown} & Lists where your tokens are going, file by file \\
\texttt{/optimize} & Finds low-relevance tabs and suggests closing them \\
\texttt{/pin} & Pins a file so it always stays in context \\
\texttt{/unpin} & Removes the pin from a file \\
\texttt{/model} & Shows which AI model is active or lets you switch \\
\texttt{/preview} & Estimates the token cost of your next message \\
\texttt{/compaction} & Shows how tokens grow with each conversation turn \\
\texttt{/instructions} & Lists instruction files and their token cost \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{VS Code Chat commands available through \texttt{@tokalator}.}
\label{tab:commands}
\end{table}

\subsection{Example: Cleaning Up Your Context}

Suppose you are working on a React component and you have 25 tabs open. You notice the
budget bar is at 70\%. You type:

\begin{lstlisting}
@tokalator /optimize
\end{lstlisting}

Tokalator checks every open tab and finds that 12 of them have a relevance score below
0.2. These are files in unrelated parts of the project that you opened earlier and forgot
to close. It suggests closing them. After you close those tabs, the budget drops to 35\%,
giving the AI model much more room to work.

\subsection{Example: Pinning Important Files}

You are working on a function in \texttt{utils.ts} that is used across the project. Even
though you are not editing it right now, you want the AI to always see it. You type:

\begin{lstlisting}
@tokalator /pin utils.ts
\end{lstlisting}

The file now has a relevance score of 1.0 and will not be suggested for removal by the
\texttt{/optimize} command.

When the MCP server is configured, you can ask Claude Code to use Tokalator tools in
plain English. Claude Code understands the request and calls the right tool for you.

\subsection{Counting Tokens in a File}

Ask Claude Code to count the tokens in any file:

\begin{lstlisting}
> How many tokens are in lib/pricing.ts?

Source:     lib/pricing.ts
Model:      Claude Sonnet 4.5
Tokenizer:  Claude BPE (Anthropic)
Tokens:     3,842
Characters: 14,219
Ratio:      ~3.7 chars/token
\end{lstlisting}

This tells you exactly how many tokens the file will consume when the AI reads it. The
ratio shows that in this file, roughly every 3.7 characters become one token.

\subsection{Checking Your Context Budget}

Ask Claude Code to estimate how much of the context window your current files use:

\begin{lstlisting}
> What is my token budget for lib/pricing.ts,
  components/Calculator.tsx, and app/page.tsx?

Model:    Claude Sonnet 4.5 (200K ctx)
Budget:   18.2K / 200K (9.1%) -- COMFORTABLE

Breakdown:
  Files:          ~12.2K    6.1%
  System prompt:  ~ 2.0K    1.0%
  Instructions:   ~ 0.0K    0.0%
  Conversation:   ~   0K    0.0%
  Output reserve: ~ 4.0K    2.0%
\end{lstlisting}

The breakdown shows that the three files use 12,200 tokens, the system prompt uses about
2,000, and 4,000 tokens are reserved for the model's response. Together, that is 9.1\%
of the 200,000 token window. The status says COMFORTABLE, meaning there is plenty of
room.

\subsection{Previewing a Turn Before Sending}

Before you paste a large block of code into the chat, you can ask Claude Code to preview
how much it would cost:

\begin{lstlisting}
> Preview the token cost if I send this 500-line file

Estimated input:  ~4,200 tokens
Estimated cost:   ~$0.013 (Claude Sonnet 4.5)
Budget after:     22.4K / 200K (11.2%)
\end{lstlisting}

This lets you decide whether to send the full file or just the relevant part.

\subsection{Listing Available Models}

You can ask which models Tokalator knows about:

\begin{lstlisting}
> List all available models

 1. Claude Opus 4.6     200K ctx   $5.00/$25.00 per MTok
 2. Claude Sonnet 4.5   200K ctx   $3.00/$15.00 per MTok
 3. Claude Haiku 4.5    200K ctx   $1.00/$5.00 per MTok
 4. GPT-5.4             200K ctx   ...
 5. Gemini 3.0 Pro      2M ctx     ...
    ...
\end{lstlisting}

This helps you compare context window sizes and prices when choosing a model for your
task.


\section{How Relevance Scoring Works}

When Tokalator assigns a score to an open tab, it looks at five things:

\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item \textbf{Same language.} If the tab is written in the same programming language as
    the file you are currently editing, it gets a higher score.
  \item \textbf{Import relationship.} If your active file imports or requires the tab
    file, that tab is clearly important.
  \item \textbf{Path similarity.} Files in the same folder or nearby folders are more
    likely to be related.
  \item \textbf{Recent edits.} A file you edited two minutes ago is more relevant than
    one you have not touched in an hour.
  \item \textbf{Errors and warnings.} If the tab has compiler errors, it is probably
    something you need to look at.
\end{enumerate}

The extension combines these five signals into a single number between 0 and 1. A score
of 0.8 means the file is very likely useful to the AI. A score of 0.1 means it is
probably not needed and is just taking up token space.

Pinned files always get a score of 1.0. The file you are actively editing also always
gets 1.0.


\section{Practical Tips}

Here are some habits that help you get the most out of Tokalator:

\begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item \textbf{Close tabs you are not using.} This is the simplest way to free up
    tokens. Run \texttt{/optimize} regularly to find tabs that are not relevant.
  \item \textbf{Pin files that matter.} If there is a core utility file or a type
    definition that the AI should always see, pin it.
  \item \textbf{Watch the budget after long conversations.} Each conversation turn adds
    roughly 800 tokens. After 20 turns, that is 16,000 tokens just from chat history.
    Use \texttt{/compaction} to see when it is time to start a new conversation.
  \item \textbf{Choose the right model.} If your task is simple, use a smaller model
    like Haiku. It costs five times less per token than Opus and still handles
    straightforward tasks well.
  \item \textbf{Use caching when possible.} Prompt caching with Anthropic reduces the
    cost of repeated context by up to 90\%. The web platform has a caching ROI calculator
    that shows whether caching would save you money for your usage pattern.
\end{itemize}


\section{Availability}

Tokalator is open source under the MIT license. The VS Code extension is on the Visual
Studio Marketplace. The MCP server is available through npm. The web platform is deployed
on Vercel. All source code is at \url{https://github.com/vfaraji89/tokalator}.

D.~Bergemann, A.~Bonatti, and A.~Smolin.
\newblock The Economics of Large Language Models.
\newblock \textit{Working Paper}, 2025.

\bibitem{tiktoken}
OpenAI.
\newblock tiktoken: A fast BPE tokeniser for use with OpenAI models.
\newblock \url{https://github.com/openai/tiktoken}, 2023.

\end{thebibliography}

\end{document}

This lets you decide whether to send the full file or just the relevant part.

\subsection{Listing Available Models}

You can ask which models Tokalator knows about:

\begin{lstlisting}
> List all available models

 1. Claude Opus 4.6     200K ctx   $5.00/$25.00 per MTok
 2. Claude Sonnet 4.5   200K ctx   $3.00/$15.00 per MTok
 3. Claude Haiku 4.5    200K ctx   $1.00/$5.00 per MTok
 4. GPT-5.4             200K ctx   ...
 5. Gemini 3.0 Pro      2M ctx     ...
    ...
\end{lstlisting}

This helps you compare context window sizes and prices when choosing a model for your
task.


\section{How Relevance Scoring Works}

When Tokalator assigns a score to an open tab, it looks at five things:

\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item \textbf{Same language.} If the tab is written in the same programming language as
    the file you are currently editing, it gets a higher score.
  \item \textbf{Import relationship.} If your active file imports or requires the tab
    file, that tab is clearly important.
  \item \textbf{Path similarity.} Files in the same folder or nearby folders are more
    likely to be related.
  \item \textbf{Recent edits.} A file you edited two minutes ago is more relevant than
    one you have not touched in an hour.
  \item \textbf{Errors and warnings.} If the tab has compiler errors, it is probably
    something you need to look at.
\end{enumerate}

The extension combines these five signals into a single number between 0 and 1. A score
of 0.8 means the file is very likely useful to the AI. A score of 0.1 means it is
probably not needed and is just taking up token space.

Pinned files always get a score of 1.0. The file you are actively editing also always
gets 1.0.


\section{Practical Tips}

Here are some habits that help you get the most out of Tokalator:

\begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item \textbf{Close tabs you are not using.} This is the simplest way to free up
    tokens. Run \texttt{/optimize} regularly to find tabs that are not relevant.
  \item \textbf{Pin files that matter.} If there is a core utility file or a type
    definition that the AI should always see, pin it.
  \item \textbf{Watch the budget after long conversations.} Each conversation turn adds
    roughly 800 tokens. After 20 turns, that is 16,000 tokens just from chat history.
    Use \texttt{/compaction} to see when it is time to start a new conversation.
  \item \textbf{Choose the right model.} If your task is simple, use a smaller model
    like Haiku. It costs five times less per token than Opus and still handles
    straightforward tasks well.
  \item \textbf{Use caching when possible.} Prompt caching with Anthropic reduces the
    cost of repeated context by up to 90\%. The web platform has a caching ROI calculator
    that shows whether caching would save you money for your usage pattern.
\end{itemize}


\section{Availability}

Tokalator is open source under the MIT license. The VS Code extension is on the Visual
Studio Marketplace. The MCP server is available through npm. The web platform is deployed
on Vercel. All source code is at \url{https://github.com/vfaraji89/tokalator}.

\title{Tokalator: A Practical Guide to Token Budget Monitoring\\for AI-Assisted Software Development}

\author{
  Vahid Faraji \\
  \texttt{vfaraji89@gmail.com}
}

\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
AI coding assistants read your open files, conversation history, and instructions before
they generate a response. All of this text is broken into tokens, and every model has a
limit on how many tokens it can process at once. Developers today have no easy way to
see how much of that limit they are using or how much it costs. Tokalator is an
open-source toolkit that shows you this information in real time. It has three parts: a
VS Code extension with a live dashboard, an MCP server that works inside Claude Code,
and a web platform with cost calculators. This paper explains what Tokalator is, how to
install each part, and how to use it in everyday development work.
\end{abstract}


\section{What Is Tokalator}

When you ask an AI assistant to write code or fix a bug, it does not just read your
question. It also reads the files you have open, any instruction files in your project,
and the full conversation you have had so far. The assistant converts all of this text
into small pieces called tokens. A single English word is usually one or two tokens. A
line of code might be five to ten tokens.

Every AI model has a maximum number of tokens it can handle at once. This is called the
context window. Claude Opus 4.6, for example, can handle 200,000 tokens at a time. If
your open files and conversation history use up most of that window, the model has less
room to think and produce a good answer.

On top of that, tokens cost money. Providers like Anthropic and OpenAI charge per million
tokens. If you send 50,000 input tokens to Claude Sonnet 4.5, that single request costs
about \$0.15. Over hundreds of requests per day, the cost adds up.

Tokalator makes these numbers visible. The name comes from ``token'' and ``calculator.''
It works like an abacus for your AI usage: it counts what goes in, shows you what each
piece costs, and tells you which files are actually useful to the assistant and which ones
are wasting space.


\section{The Three Components}

Tokalator has three parts. You can use any of them on their own or together.

\textbf{VS Code Extension.} A sidebar panel inside VS Code that shows a live token count,
a budget bar, and a relevance score for each open tab. It also adds a chat participant
called \texttt{@tokalator} that you can talk to inside VS Code Chat.

\textbf{MCP Server.} A small server that runs in the background and gives Claude Code
access to four tools: count tokens, estimate your budget, preview the cost of your next
message, and list available models. Claude Code loads it automatically from the project
configuration.

\textbf{Web Platform.} A website with interactive calculators where you can compare model
prices, estimate caching savings, and analyze costs for different usage patterns.


\section{How to Install}

\subsection{Installing the VS Code Extension}

Open VS Code and go to the Extensions panel. Search for ``Tokalator'' and click Install.
You can also install it from the terminal:

\begin{lstlisting}
code --install-extension vfaraji89.tokalator
\end{lstlisting}

After installation, a new icon appears in the Activity Bar on the left side of VS Code.
Click it to open the Tokalator sidebar.

\subsection{Setting Up the MCP Server}

The MCP server lets Claude Code use Tokalator tools directly in the terminal. To set it
up, add the following to the \texttt{.mcp.json} file in your project root:

\begin{lstlisting}
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "tokalator": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "tokalator-mcp@latest"]
    }
  }
}
\end{lstlisting}

The next time you start Claude Code in that project, it will load the Tokalator tools
automatically. You do not need to run any extra commands.

\subsection{Using the Web Platform}

Visit the Tokalator website to use the online calculators. No installation is needed.
The site includes a token cost calculator, a caching ROI estimator, a model comparison
table, and a conversation budget planner.


\section{How to Use the VS Code Extension}

Once installed, the extension starts working right away. Here is what you can do with it.

\subsection{Reading the Sidebar Dashboard}

The sidebar shows three things at a glance:

\begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item \textbf{Budget bar.} A progress bar that fills up as you use more tokens. It
    shows how much of the model's context window you have used. Green means comfortable,
    yellow means you are getting close to the limit, and red means you are near full.
  \item \textbf{Token breakdown.} A list that shows where your tokens are going: open
    files, system prompt, instruction files, conversation history, and output reservation.
  \item \textbf{Tab list with scores.} Every open tab appears with its token count and a
    relevance score from 0 to 1. A score near 1 means the file is important to the
    assistant. A score near 0 means it is probably not needed.
\end{itemize}

The dashboard updates every time you open, close, or edit a file. You do not need to
refresh anything.

\subsection{Using Chat Commands}

Type \texttt{@tokalator} in VS Code Chat followed by a command. Here are the most useful
ones:

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lp{7.5cm}@{}}
\toprule
Command & What it does \\
\midrule
\texttt{/count} & Shows the total token count and budget status \\
\texttt{/breakdown} & Lists where your tokens are going, file by file \\
\texttt{/optimize} & Finds low-relevance tabs and suggests closing them \\
\texttt{/pin} & Pins a file so it always stays in context \\
\texttt{/unpin} & Removes the pin from a file \\
\texttt{/model} & Shows which AI model is active or lets you switch \\
\texttt{/preview} & Estimates the token cost of your next message \\
\texttt{/compaction} & Shows how tokens grow with each conversation turn \\
\texttt{/instructions} & Lists instruction files and their token cost \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{VS Code Chat commands available through \texttt{@tokalator}.}
\label{tab:commands}
\end{table}

\subsection{Example: Cleaning Up Your Context}

Suppose you are working on a React component and you have 25 tabs open. You notice the
budget bar is at 70\%. You type:

\begin{lstlisting}
@tokalator /optimize
\end{lstlisting}

Tokalator checks every open tab and finds that 12 of them have a relevance score below
0.2. These are files in unrelated parts of the project that you opened earlier and forgot
to close. It suggests closing them. After you close those tabs, the budget drops to 35\%,
giving the AI model much more room to work.

\subsection{Example: Pinning Important Files}

You are working on a function in \texttt{utils.ts} that is used across the project. Even
though you are not editing it right now, you want the AI to always see it. You type:

\begin{lstlisting}
@tokalator /pin utils.ts
\end{lstlisting}

The file now has a relevance score of 1.0 and will not be suggested for removal by the
\texttt{/optimize} command.


\section{How to Use the MCP Server in Claude Code}

When the MCP server is configured, you can ask Claude Code to use Tokalator tools in
plain English. Claude Code understands the request and calls the right tool for you.

\subsection{Counting Tokens in a File}

Ask Claude Code to count the tokens in any file:

\begin{lstlisting}
> How many tokens are in lib/pricing.ts?

Source:     lib/pricing.ts
Model:      Claude Sonnet 4.5
Tokenizer:  Claude BPE (Anthropic)
Tokens:     3,842
Characters: 14,219
Ratio:      ~3.7 chars/token
\end{lstlisting}

This tells you exactly how many tokens the file will consume when the AI reads it. The
ratio shows that in this file, roughly every 3.7 characters become one token.

\subsection{Checking Your Context Budget}

Ask Claude Code to estimate how much of the context window your current files use:

\begin{lstlisting}
> What is my token budget for lib/pricing.ts,
  components/Calculator.tsx, and app/page.tsx?

Model:    Claude Sonnet 4.5 (200K ctx)
Budget:   18.2K / 200K (9.1%) -- COMFORTABLE

Breakdown:
  Files:          ~12.2K    6.1%
  System prompt:  ~ 2.0K    1.0%
  Instructions:   ~ 0.0K    0.0%
  Conversation:   ~   0K    0.0%
  Output reserve: ~ 4.0K    2.0%
\end{lstlisting}

The breakdown shows that the three files use 12,200 tokens, the system prompt uses about
2,000, and 4,000 tokens are reserved for the model's response. Together, that is 9.1\%
of the 200,000 token window. The status says COMFORTABLE, meaning there is plenty of
room.

\subsection{Previewing a Turn Before Sending}

Once installed, the extension starts working right away. Here is what you can do with it.

\subsection{Reading the Sidebar Dashboard}

The sidebar shows three things at a glance:

\begin{itemize}[]
  \item \textbf{Budget bar.} A progress bar that fills up as you use more tokens. It
    shows how much of the model's context window you have used. Green means comfortable,
    yellow means you are getting close to the limit, and red means you are near full.
  \item \textbf{Token breakdown.} A list that shows where your tokens are going: open
    files, system prompt, instruction files, conversation history, and output reservation.
  \item \textbf{Tab list with scores.} Every open tab appears with its token count and a
    relevance score from 0 to 1. A score near 1 means the file is important to the
    assistant. A score near 0 means it is probably not needed.
\end{itemize}

The dashboard updates every time you open, close, or edit a file. You do not need to
refresh anything.

\subsection{Using Chat Commands}

Type \texttt{@tokalator} in VS Code Chat followed by a command. Here are the most useful
ones:

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lp{7.5cm}@{}}
\toprule
Command & What it does \\
\midrule
\texttt{/count} & Shows the total token count and budget status \\
\texttt{/breakdown} & Lists where your tokens are going, file by file \\
\texttt{/optimize} & Finds low-relevance tabs and suggests closing them \\
\texttt{/pin} & Pins a file so it always stays in context \\
\texttt{/unpin} & Removes the pin from a file \\
\texttt{/model} & Shows which AI model is active or lets you switch \\
\texttt{/preview} & Estimates the token cost of your next message \\
\texttt{/compaction} & Shows how tokens grow with each conversation turn \\
\texttt{/instructions} & Lists instruction files and their token cost \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{VS Code Chat commands available through \texttt{@tokalator}.}
\label{tab:commands}
\end{table}

\subsection{Example: Cleaning Up Your Context}

Suppose you are working on a React component and you have 25 tabs open. You notice the
budget bar is at 70\%. You type:

\begin{lstlisting}
@tokalator /optimize
\end{lstlisting}

Tokalator checks every open tab and finds that 12 of them have a relevance score below
0.2. These are files in unrelated parts of the project that you opened earlier and forgot
to close. It suggests closing them. After you close those tabs, the budget drops to 35\%,
giving the AI model much more room to work.

\subsection{Example: Pinning Important Files}

You are working on a function in \texttt{utils.ts} that is used across the project. Even
though you are not editing it right now, you want the AI to always see it. You type:

\begin{lstlisting}
@tokalator /pin utils.ts
\end{lstlisting}

The file now has a relevance score of 1.0 and will not be suggested for removal by the
\texttt{/optimize} command.


\section{How to Use the MCP Server in Claude Code}

When the MCP server is configured, you can ask Claude Code to use Tokalator tools in
plain English. Claude Code understands the request and calls the right tool for you.

\subsection{Counting Tokens in a File}

Ask Claude Code to count the tokens in any file:

\begin{lstlisting}
> How many tokens are in lib/pricing.ts?

Source:     lib/pricing.ts
Model:      Claude Sonnet 4.5
Tokenizer:  Claude BPE (Anthropic)
Tokens:     3,842
Characters: 14,219
Ratio:      ~3.7 chars/token
\end{lstlisting}

This tells you exactly how many tokens the file will consume when the AI reads it. The
ratio shows that in this file, roughly every 3.7 characters become one token.

\subsection{Checking Your Context Budget}

Ask Claude Code to estimate how much of the context window your current files use:

\begin{lstlisting}
> What is my token budget for lib/pricing.ts,
  components/Calculator.tsx, and app/page.tsx?

Model:    Claude Sonnet 4.5 (200K ctx)
Budget:   18.2K / 200K (9.1%) -- COMFORTABLE

Breakdown:
  Files:          ~12.2K    6.1%
  System prompt:  ~ 2.0K    1.0%
  Instructions:   ~ 0.0K    0.0%
  Conversation:   ~   0K    0.0%
  Output reserve: ~ 4.0K    2.0%
\end{lstlisting}

The breakdown shows that the three files use 12,200 tokens, the system prompt uses about
2,000, and 4,000 tokens are reserved for the model's response. Together, that is 9.1\%
of the 200,000 token window. The status says COMFORTABLE, meaning there is plenty of
room.

\subsection{Previewing a Turn Before Sending}

Before you paste a large block of code into the chat, you can ask Claude Code to preview
how much it would cost:

\begin{lstlisting}
> Preview the token cost if I send this 500-line file

Estimated input:  ~4,200 tokens
Estimated cost:   ~$0.013 (Claude Sonnet 4.5)
Budget after:     22.4K / 200K (11.2%)
\end{lstlisting}

This lets you decide whether to send the full file or just the relevant part.

\subsection{Listing Available Models}

You can ask which models Tokalator knows about:

\begin{lstlisting}
> List all available models

 1. Claude Opus 4.6     200K ctx   $5.00/$25.00 per MTok
 2. Claude Sonnet 4.5   200K ctx   $3.00/$15.00 per MTok
 3. Claude Haiku 4.5    200K ctx   $1.00/$5.00 per MTok
 4. GPT-5.4             200K ctx   ...
 5. Gemini 3.0 Pro      2M ctx     ...
    ...
\end{lstlisting}

This helps you compare context window sizes and prices when choosing a model for your
task.


\section{How Relevance Scoring Works}

When Tokalator assigns a score to an open tab, it looks at five things:

\begin{enumerate}[]
  \item \textbf{Same language.} If the tab is written in the same programming language as
    the file you are currently editing, it gets a higher score.
  \item \textbf{Import relationship.} If your active file imports or requires the tab
    file, that tab is clearly important.
  \item \textbf{Path similarity.} Files in the same folder or nearby folders are more
    likely to be related.
  \item \textbf{Recent edits.} A file you edited two minutes ago is more relevant than
    one you have not touched in an hour.
  \item \textbf{Errors and warnings.} If the tab has compiler errors, it is probably
    something you need to look at.
\end{enumerate}

The extension combines these five signals into a single number between 0 and 1. A score
of 0.8 means the file is very likely useful to the AI. A score of 0.1 means it is
probably not needed and is just taking up token space.

Pinned files always get a score of 1.0. The file you are actively editing also always
gets 1.0.


\section{Practical Tips}

Here are some habits that help you get the most out of Tokalator:

\begin{itemize}[]
  \item \textbf{Close tabs you are not using.} This is the simplest way to free up
    tokens. Run \texttt{/optimize} regularly to find tabs that are not relevant.
  \item \textbf{Pin files that matter.} If there is a core utility file or a type
    definition that the AI should always see, pin it.
  \item \textbf{Watch the budget after long conversations.} Each conversation turn adds
    roughly 800 tokens. After 20 turns, that is 16,000 tokens just from chat history.
    Use \texttt{/compaction} to see when it is time to start a new conversation.
  \item \textbf{Choose the right model.} If your task is simple, use a smaller model
    like Haiku. It costs five times less per token than Opus and still handles
    straightforward tasks well.
  \item \textbf{Use caching when possible.} Prompt caching with Anthropic reduces the
    cost of repeated context by up to 90\%. The web platform has a caching ROI calculator
    that shows whether caching would save you money for your usage pattern.
\end{itemize}


\section{Availability}

Tokalator is open source under the MIT license. The VS Code extension is on the Visual
Studio Marketplace. The MCP server is available through npm. The web platform is deployed
on Vercel. All source code is at \url{https://github.com/vfaraji89/tokalator}.


\begin{thebibliography}{9}

\bibitem{bergemann2025}
D.~Bergemann, A.~Bonatti, and A.~Smolin.
\newblock The Economics of Large Language Models.
\newblock \textit{Working Paper}, 2025.

\bibitem{tiktoken}
OpenAI.
\newblock tiktoken: A fast BPE tokeniser for use with OpenAI models.
\newblock \url{https://github.com/openai/tiktoken}, 2023.

\end{thebibliography}

\section{The Three Components}

\end{itemize}

Studio Marketplace. The MCP server is available through npm. The web platform is deployed
on Vercel. All source code is at \url{https://github.com/vfaraji89/tokalator}.

1	\documentclass[11pt,a4paper]{article}
2	\usepackage[margin=2.2cm]{geometry}
3	\usepackage{times}

14	\definecolor{codetext}{rgb}{0.2,0.2,0.2}
15

17	  backgroundcolor=\color{codebg},
18	  basicstyle=\small\ttfamily\color{codetext},
19	  breaklines=true,
20	  frame=single,
21	  rulecolor=\color{black!30},
22	  xleftmargin=4pt,
23	  xrightmargin=4pt,
24	  aboveskip=6pt,
25	  belowskip=6pt,
26	}

28	\title{Tokalator: A Practical Guide to Token Budget Monitoring\\for AI-Assisted Software Development}
29	
30	\author{
31	  Vahid Faraji \\
32	  \texttt{vfaraji89@gmail.com}
33	}
34	
35	\date{}
36	
37	\begin{document}
38	\maketitle
39	
40	\begin{abstract}
41	AI coding assistants read your open files, conversation history, and instructions before
42	they generate a response. All of this text is broken into tokens, and every model has a
43	limit on how many tokens it can process at once. Developers today have no easy way to
44	see how much of that limit they are using or how much it costs. Tokalator is an
45	open-source toolkit that shows you this information in real time. It has three parts: a
46	VS Code extension with a live dashboard, an MCP server that works inside Claude Code,
47	and a web platform with cost calculators. This paper explains what Tokalator is, how to
48	install each part, and how to use it in everyday development work.
49	\end{abstract}
50	
51	
52	\section{What Is Tokalator}
53	
54	When you ask an AI assistant to write code or fix a bug, it reads your open files,
55	instruction files, and the full conversation so far. The assistant converts all of this
56	text into small pieces called tokens. A single English word is usually one or two tokens.
57	A line of code might be five to ten tokens.
58	
59	Every AI model has a maximum number of tokens it can handle at once, called the context
60	window. Claude Opus 4.6 can handle 200,000 tokens. If your open files and conversation
61	use up most of that window, the model has less room to produce a good answer. Tokens also
62	cost money. Providers charge per million tokens. Over hundreds of requests per day, the
63	cost adds up.
64	
65	Tokalator makes these numbers visible. The name comes from ``token'' and ``calculator.''
66	It counts what goes in, shows you what each piece costs, and tells you which files are
67	useful to the assistant and which ones are wasting space.
68	
69	
70	\section{The Three Components}
71	
72	Tokalator has three parts. You can use any of them on their own or together.
73	(1)~\textbf{VS Code Extension}: a sidebar panel that shows a live token count, a budget
74	bar, and a relevance score for each open tab, plus a chat participant
75	(\texttt{@tokalator}) for commands.
76	(2)~\textbf{MCP Server}: a background server that gives Claude Code four tools (count
77	tokens, estimate budget, preview cost, list models), loaded automatically from the
78	project configuration.
79	(3)~\textbf{Web Platform}: a website with interactive calculators for comparing model
80	prices, estimating caching savings, and analyzing costs.
81	
82	
83	\section{How to Install}
84	
85	\subsection{Installing the VS Code Extension}
86	
87	Open VS Code and go to the Extensions panel. Search for ``Tokalator'' and click Install.
88	You can also install it from the terminal:
89	
90	\begin{lstlisting}
91	code --install-extension vfaraji89.tokalator
92	\end{lstlisting}
93	
94	After installation, a new icon appears in the Activity Bar on the left side of VS Code.
95	Click it to open the Tokalator sidebar.
96	
97	\subsection{Setting Up the MCP Server}
98	
99	The MCP server lets Claude Code use Tokalator tools directly in the terminal. To set it
100	up, add the following to the \texttt{.mcp.json} file in your project root:
101	
102	\begin{lstlisting}
103	{
104	  "mcpServers": {
105	    "tokalator": {
106	      "command": "npx",
107	      "args": ["-y", "tokalator-mcp@latest"]
108	    }
109	  }
110	}
111	\end{lstlisting}
112	
113	The next time you start Claude Code in that project, it will load the Tokalator tools
114	automatically. You do not need to run any extra commands.
115	
116	\subsection{Using the Web Platform}
117	
118	Visit the Tokalator website to use the online calculators. No installation is needed.
119	
120	
121	\section{How to Use the VS Code Extension}
122	
123	Once installed, the extension starts working right away. Here is what you can do with it.
124	
125	\subsection{Reading the Sidebar Dashboard}
126	
127	The sidebar shows three things at a glance:
128	
129	\begin{itemize}[]
130	  \item \textbf{Budget bar.} A progress bar that fills up as you use more tokens. It
131	    shows how much of the model's context window you have used. Green means comfortable,
132	    yellow means you are getting close to the limit, and red means you are near full.
133	  \item \textbf{Token breakdown.} A list that shows where your tokens are going: open
134	    files, system prompt, instruction files, conversation history, and output reservation.
135	  \item \textbf{Tab list with scores.} Every open tab appears with its token count and a
136	    relevance score from 0 to 1. A score near 1 means the file is important to the
137	    assistant. A score near 0 means it is probably not needed.
138	\end{itemize}
139	
140	The dashboard updates every time you open, close, or edit a file. You do not need to
141	refresh anything.
142	
143	\subsection{Using Chat Commands}
144	
145	Type \texttt{@tokalator} in VS Code Chat followed by a command. Here are the most useful
146	ones:
147	
148	\begin{table}[H]
149	\centering
150	\small
151	\begin{tabular}{@{}lp{7.5cm}@{}}
152	\toprule
153	Command & What it does \\
154	\midrule
155	\texttt{/count} & Shows the total token count and budget status \\
156	\texttt{/breakdown} & Lists where your tokens are going, file by file \\
157	\texttt{/optimize} & Finds low-relevance tabs and suggests closing them \\
158	\texttt{/pin} & Pins a file so it always stays in context \\
159	\texttt{/unpin} & Removes the pin from a file \\
160	\texttt{/model} & Shows which AI model is active or lets you switch \\
161	\texttt{/preview} & Estimates the token cost of your next message \\
162	\texttt{/compaction} & Shows how tokens grow with each conversation turn \\
163	\texttt{/instructions} & Lists instruction files and their token cost \\
164	\bottomrule
165	\end{tabular}
166	\caption{VS Code Chat commands available through \texttt{@tokalator}.}
167	\label{tab:commands}
168	\end{table}
169	
170	\subsection{Example: Cleaning Up Your Context}
171	
172	Suppose you are working on a React component and you have 25 tabs open. You notice the
173	budget bar is at 70\%. You type:
174	
175	\begin{lstlisting}
176	@tokalator /optimize
177	\end{lstlisting}
178	
179	Tokalator checks every open tab and finds that 12 of them have a relevance score below
180	0.2. These are files in unrelated parts of the project that you opened earlier and forgot
181	to close. It suggests closing them. After you close those tabs, the budget drops to 35\%,
182	giving the AI model much more room to work.
183	
184	\subsection{Example: Pinning Important Files}
185	
186	You are working on a function in \texttt{utils.ts} that is used across the project. Even
187	though you are not editing it right now, you want the AI to always see it. You type:
188	
189	\begin{lstlisting}
190	@tokalator /pin utils.ts
191	\end{lstlisting}
192	
193	The file now has a relevance score of 1.0 and will not be suggested for removal by the
194	\texttt{/optimize} command.
195	
196	
197	\section{How to Use the MCP Server in Claude Code}
198	
199	When the MCP server is configured, you can ask Claude Code to use Tokalator tools in
200	plain English. Claude Code understands the request and calls the right tool for you.
201	
202	\subsection{Counting Tokens in a File}
203	
204	Ask Claude Code to count the tokens in any file:
205	
206	\begin{lstlisting}
207	> How many tokens are in lib/pricing.ts?
208	
209	Source:     lib/pricing.ts
210	Model:      Claude Sonnet 4.5
211	Tokenizer:  Claude BPE (Anthropic)
212	Tokens:     3,842
213	Characters: 14,219
214	Ratio:      ~3.7 chars/token
215	\end{lstlisting}
216	
217	The ratio shows that roughly every 3.7 characters become one token in this file.
218	
219	\subsection{Checking Your Context Budget}
220	
221	\begin{lstlisting}
222	> What is my token budget for lib/pricing.ts,
223	  components/Calculator.tsx, and app/page.tsx?
224	
225	Model:    Claude Sonnet 4.5 (200K ctx)
226	Budget:   18.2K / 200K (9.1%) -- COMFORTABLE
227	
228	Breakdown:
229	  Files:          ~12.2K    6.1%
230	  System prompt:  ~ 2.0K    1.0%
231	  Instructions:   ~ 0.0K    0.0%
232	  Conversation:   ~   0K    0.0%
233	  Output reserve: ~ 4.0K    2.0%
234	\end{lstlisting}
235	
236	The three files use 12,200 tokens. Together with the system prompt and output
237	reservation, that is 9.1\% of the 200,000 token window. The status COMFORTABLE means
238	there is plenty of room.
239	
240	\subsection{Previewing a Turn Before Sending}
241	
242	Before you paste a large block of code into the chat, you can ask Claude Code to preview
243	how much it would cost:
244	
245	\begin{lstlisting}
246	> Preview the token cost if I send this 500-line file
247	
248	Estimated input:  ~4,200 tokens
249	Estimated cost:   ~$0.013 (Claude Sonnet 4.5)
250	Budget after:     22.4K / 200K (11.2%)
251	\end{lstlisting}
252	
253	This lets you decide whether to send the full file or just the relevant part.
254	
255	\subsection{Listing Available Models}
256	
257	You can ask which models Tokalator knows about. It returns each model with its context
258	window size and per-million-token prices, helping you compare options before starting a
259	task.
260	
261	
262	\section{How Relevance Scoring Works}
263	
264	When Tokalator assigns a score to an open tab, it checks five signals: (1) whether the
265	tab shares the same programming language as your active file, (2) whether your active
266	file imports the tab file, (3) whether they are in the same or nearby folders, (4) how
267	recently you edited the tab, and (5) whether the tab has compiler errors or warnings.
268	These signals are combined into a single number between 0 and 1. A score of 0.8 means
269	the file is very likely useful to the AI. A score of 0.1 means it is probably not needed.
270	Pinned files and the active editor always get a score of 1.0.
271	
272	
273	\section{Practical Tips}
274	
275	\textbf{Close tabs you are not using.} Run \texttt{/optimize} regularly to find
276	irrelevant tabs. \textbf{Pin files that matter.} Core utility files or type definitions
277	the AI should always see can be pinned with \texttt{/pin}. \textbf{Watch the budget
278	after long conversations.} Each turn adds roughly 800 tokens; after 20 turns, that is
279	16,000 tokens from chat history alone. Use \texttt{/compaction} to check when to start
280	fresh. \textbf{Choose the right model.} Haiku costs five times less per token than Opus
281	and handles straightforward tasks well. \textbf{Use caching.} Prompt caching with
282	Anthropic reduces repeated context cost by up to 90\%.
283	
284	\section{Availability}
285	
286	Tokalator is open source (MIT license). The VS Code extension is on the Visual Studio
287	Marketplace, the MCP server on npm, and the web platform on Vercel.
288	Source: \url{https://github.com/vfaraji89/tokalator}.
289	
290	
291	\begin{thebibliography}{9}
292	
293	\bibitem{bergemann2025}
294	D.~Bergemann, A.~Bonatti, and A.~Smolin.
295	\newblock The Economics of Large Language Models.
296	\newblock \textit{Working Paper}, 2025.
297	
298	\bibitem{tiktoken}
299	OpenAI.
300	\newblock tiktoken: A fast BPE tokeniser for use with OpenAI models.
301	\newblock \url{https://github.com/openai/tiktoken}, 2023.
302	
303	\end{thebibliography}
304	
305	\end{document}

Tokalator makes these numbers visible. The name comes from ``token'' and ``calculator.''
It counts what goes in, shows you what each piece costs, and tells you which files are
useful to the assistant and which ones are wasting space.


\section{Why Token Visibility Matters}

Token monitoring is not just about saving money. It is about understanding a hard
constraint that affects every interaction with an AI model. There are three separate
limits that developers need to be aware of, and all three are measured in tokens.

\textbf{Context window limits.} Every model has a fixed context window. When the total
input exceeds that window, the oldest parts of the conversation or the least recent
files get dropped silently. The developer does not receive a warning. The model simply
works with less information and may produce a worse answer. A developer who monitors
token usage can see when the window is getting full and take action before the model
starts losing context.

\textbf{Usage and rate limits.} Providers impose limits on how many tokens a user can
send within a given time period. Anthropic, for example, sets per-minute and daily token
caps that vary by subscription tier. Claude Pro users have a lower daily allowance than
Claude Max users. OpenAI applies similar rate limits on its API and ChatGPT plans. When
a developer hits a rate limit, the service stops responding until the limit resets. This
can interrupt work for minutes or hours. Without visibility into how many tokens each
request consumes, developers have no way to predict when they will hit the wall. A
single large request that sends 80,000 tokens of file context can use up a significant
part of the daily allowance in one turn.

\textbf{Cost accumulation.} For API users who pay per token, costs grow with every
request. Input tokens, output tokens, cache writes, and cache reads each have a
separate price. A team of five developers each making 100 requests per day can generate
millions of tokens daily. Without a tool that shows where those tokens come from, it is
difficult to find which files, which conversations, or which workflows are responsible
for the highest costs.

The core problem is that tokens are invisible by default. The editor does not show them.
The API response includes token counts in metadata, but most developers do not inspect
that metadata after every call. Tokalator brings this information to the surface so that
developers can make informed decisions: close unnecessary tabs before a request, start a
new conversation when the old one is too long, switch to a cheaper model for simple
tasks, or use prompt caching to avoid resending the same context repeatedly.


\section{The Three Components}

\title{Tokalator: A Practical Guide to Token Budget Monitoring\\for AI-Assisted Software Development}

\author{
  Vahid Faraji \\
  \texttt{vfaraji89@gmail.com}
}

\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
AI coding assistants read your open files, conversation history, and instructions before
they generate a response. All of this text is broken into tokens, and every model has a
limit on how many tokens it can process at once. Developers today have no easy way to
see how much of that limit they are using or how much it costs. Tokalator is an
open-source toolkit that shows you this information in real time. It has three parts: a
VS Code extension with a live dashboard, an MCP server that works inside Claude Code,
and a web platform with cost calculators. This paper explains what Tokalator is, how to
install each part, and how to use it in everyday development work.
\end{abstract}


\section{What Is Tokalator}

When you ask an AI assistant to write code or fix a bug, it reads your open files,
instruction files, and the full conversation so far. The assistant converts all of this
text into small pieces called tokens. A single English word is usually one or two tokens.
A line of code might be five to ten tokens.

Every AI model has a maximum number of tokens it can handle at once, called the context
window. Claude Opus 4.6 can handle 200,000 tokens. If your open files and conversation
use up most of that window, the model has less room to produce a good answer. Tokens also
cost money. Providers charge per million tokens. Over hundreds of requests per day, the
cost adds up.

Tokalator makes these numbers visible. The name comes from ``token'' and ``calculator.''
It counts what goes in, shows you what each piece costs, and tells you which files are
useful to the assistant and which ones are wasting space.


\section{Why Token Visibility Matters}

Token monitoring is not just about saving money. It is about understanding a hard
constraint that affects every interaction with an AI model. There are three separate
limits that developers need to be aware of, and all three are measured in tokens.

\textbf{Context window limits.} Every model has a fixed context window. When the total
input exceeds that window, the oldest parts of the conversation or the least recent
files get dropped silently. The developer does not receive a warning. The model simply
works with less information and may produce a worse answer. A developer who monitors
token usage can see when the window is getting full and take action before the model
starts losing context.

\textbf{Usage and rate limits.} Providers impose limits on how many tokens a user can
send within a given time period. Anthropic, for example, sets per-minute and daily token
caps that vary by subscription tier. Claude Pro users have a lower daily allowance than
Claude Max users. OpenAI applies similar rate limits on its API and ChatGPT plans. When
a developer hits a rate limit, the service stops responding until the limit resets. This
can interrupt work for minutes or hours. Without visibility into how many tokens each
request consumes, developers have no way to predict when they will hit the wall. A
single large request that sends 80,000 tokens of file context can use up a significant
part of the daily allowance in one turn.

\textbf{Cost accumulation.} For API users who pay per token, costs grow with every
request. Input tokens, output tokens, cache writes, and cache reads each have a
separate price. A team of five developers each making 100 requests per day can generate
millions of tokens daily. Without a tool that shows where those tokens come from, it is
difficult to find which files, which conversations, or which workflows are responsible
for the highest costs.

The core problem is that tokens are invisible by default. The editor does not show them.
The API response includes token counts in metadata, but most developers do not inspect
that metadata after every call. Tokalator brings this information to the surface so that
developers can make informed decisions: close unnecessary tabs before a request, start a
new conversation when the old one is too long, switch to a cheaper model for simple
tasks, or use prompt caching to avoid resending the same context repeatedly.


\section{The Three Components}

Tokalator has three parts. You can use any of them on their own or together.
(1)~\textbf{VS Code Extension}: a sidebar panel that shows a live token count, a budget
bar, and a relevance score for each open tab, plus a chat participant
(\texttt{@tokalator}) for commands.
(2)~\textbf{MCP Server}: a background server that gives Claude Code four tools (count
tokens, estimate budget, preview cost, list models), loaded automatically from the
project configuration.
(3)~\textbf{Web Platform}: a website with interactive calculators for comparing model
prices, estimating caching savings, and analyzing costs.


\section{How to Install}

\subsection{Installing the VS Code Extension}

Open VS Code and go to the Extensions panel. Search for ``Tokalator'' and click Install.
You can also install it from the terminal:

\begin{lstlisting}
code --install-extension vfaraji89.tokalator
\end{lstlisting}

After installation, a new icon appears in the Activity Bar on the left side of VS Code.
Click it to open the Tokalator sidebar.

\subsection{Setting Up the MCP Server}

The MCP server lets Claude Code use Tokalator tools directly in the terminal. To set it
up, add the following to the \texttt{.mcp.json} file in your project root:

\begin{lstlisting}
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "tokalator": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "tokalator-mcp@latest"]
    }
  }
}
\end{lstlisting}

The next time you start Claude Code in that project, it will load the Tokalator tools
automatically. You do not need to run any extra commands.

\subsection{Using the Web Platform}

Visit the Tokalator website to use the online calculators. No installation is needed.


\section{How to Use the VS Code Extension}

Once installed, the extension starts working right away. Here is what you can do with it.

\subsection{Reading the Sidebar Dashboard}

The sidebar shows three things at a glance:

\begin{itemize}[]
  \item \textbf{Budget bar.} A progress bar that fills up as you use more tokens. It
    shows how much of the model's context window you have used. Green means comfortable,
    yellow means you are getting close to the limit, and red means you are near full.
  \item \textbf{Token breakdown.} A list that shows where your tokens are going: open
    files, system prompt, instruction files, conversation history, and output reservation.
  \item \textbf{Tab list with scores.} Every open tab appears with its token count and a
    relevance score from 0 to 1. A score near 1 means the file is important to the
    assistant. A score near 0 means it is probably not needed.
\end{itemize}

The dashboard updates every time you open, close, or edit a file. You do not need to
refresh anything.

\subsection{Using Chat Commands}

Type \texttt{@tokalator} in VS Code Chat followed by a command. Here are the most useful
ones:

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lp{7.5cm}@{}}
\toprule
Command & What it does \\
\midrule
\texttt{/count} & Shows the total token count and budget status \\
\texttt{/breakdown} & Lists where your tokens are going, file by file \\
\texttt{/optimize} & Finds low-relevance tabs and suggests closing them \\
\texttt{/pin} & Pins a file so it always stays in context \\
\texttt{/unpin} & Removes the pin from a file \\
\texttt{/model} & Shows which AI model is active or lets you switch \\
\texttt{/preview} & Estimates the token cost of your next message \\
\texttt{/compaction} & Shows how tokens grow with each conversation turn \\
\texttt{/instructions} & Lists instruction files and their token cost \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{VS Code Chat commands available through \texttt{@tokalator}.}
\label{tab:commands}
\end{table}

\subsection{Example: Cleaning Up Your Context}

Suppose you are working on a React component and you have 25 tabs open. You notice the
budget bar is at 70\%. You type:

\begin{lstlisting}
@tokalator /optimize
\end{lstlisting}

Tokalator checks every open tab and finds that 12 of them have a relevance score below
0.2. These are files in unrelated parts of the project that you opened earlier and forgot
to close. It suggests closing them. After you close those tabs, the budget drops to 35\%,
giving the AI model much more room to work.

\subsection{Example: Pinning Important Files}

You are working on a function in \texttt{utils.ts} that is used across the project. Even
though you are not editing it right now, you want the AI to always see it. You type:

\begin{lstlisting}
@tokalator /pin utils.ts
\end{lstlisting}

The file now has a relevance score of 1.0 and will not be suggested for removal by the
\texttt{/optimize} command.


\section{How to Use the MCP Server in Claude Code}

When the MCP server is configured, you can ask Claude Code to use Tokalator tools in
plain English. Claude Code understands the request and calls the right tool for you.

\subsection{Counting Tokens in a File}

Ask Claude Code to count the tokens in any file:

\begin{lstlisting}
> How many tokens are in lib/pricing.ts?

Source:     lib/pricing.ts
Model:      Claude Sonnet 4.5
Tokenizer:  Claude BPE (Anthropic)
Tokens:     3,842
Characters: 14,219
Ratio:      ~3.7 chars/token
\end{lstlisting}

The ratio shows that roughly every 3.7 characters become one token in this file.

\subsection{Checking Your Context Budget}

\begin{lstlisting}
> What is my token budget for lib/pricing.ts,
  components/Calculator.tsx, and app/page.tsx?

Model:    Claude Sonnet 4.5 (200K ctx)
Budget:   18.2K / 200K (9.1%) -- COMFORTABLE

Breakdown:
  Files:          ~12.2K    6.1%
  System prompt:  ~ 2.0K    1.0%
  Instructions:   ~ 0.0K    0.0%
  Conversation:   ~   0K    0.0%
  Output reserve: ~ 4.0K    2.0%
\end{lstlisting}

The three files use 12,200 tokens. Together with the system prompt and output
reservation, that is 9.1\% of the 200,000 token window. The status COMFORTABLE means
there is plenty of room.

\subsection{Previewing a Turn Before Sending}

Before you paste a large block of code into the chat, you can ask Claude Code to preview
how much it would cost:

\begin{lstlisting}
> Preview the token cost if I send this 500-line file

Estimated input:  ~4,200 tokens
Estimated cost:   ~$0.013 (Claude Sonnet 4.5)
Budget after:     22.4K / 200K (11.2%)
\end{lstlisting}

This lets you decide whether to send the full file or just the relevant part.

\subsection{Listing Available Models}

You can ask which models Tokalator knows about. It returns each model with its context
window size and per-million-token prices, helping you compare options before starting a
task.


\section{How Relevance Scoring Works}

When Tokalator assigns a score to an open tab, it checks five signals: (1) whether the
tab shares the same programming language as your active file, (2) whether your active
file imports the tab file, (3) whether they are in the same or nearby folders, (4) how
recently you edited the tab, and (5) whether the tab has compiler errors or warnings.
These signals are combined into a single number between 0 and 1. A score of 0.8 means
the file is very likely useful to the AI. A score of 0.1 means it is probably not needed.
Pinned files and the active editor always get a score of 1.0.


\section{Practical Tips}

\textbf{Close tabs you are not using.} Run \texttt{/optimize} regularly to find
irrelevant tabs. \textbf{Pin files that matter.} Core utility files or type definitions
the AI should always see can be pinned with \texttt{/pin}. \textbf{Watch the budget
after long conversations.} Each turn adds roughly 800 tokens; after 20 turns, that is
16,000 tokens from chat history alone. Use \texttt{/compaction} to check when to start
fresh. \textbf{Choose the right model.} Haiku costs five times less per token than Opus
and handles straightforward tasks well. \textbf{Use caching.} Prompt caching with
Anthropic reduces repeated context cost by up to 90\%.

\section{Availability}

Tokalator is open source (MIT license). The VS Code extension is on the Visual Studio
Marketplace, the MCP server on npm, and the web platform on Vercel.
Source: \url{https://github.com/vfaraji89/tokalator}.


\begin{thebibliography}{9}

\bibitem{bergemann2025}
D.~Bergemann, A.~Bonatti, and A.~Smolin.
\newblock The Economics of Large Language Models.
\newblock \textit{Working Paper}, 2025.

\bibitem{tiktoken}
OpenAI.
\newblock tiktoken: A fast BPE tokeniser for use with OpenAI models.
\newblock \url{https://github.com/openai/tiktoken}, 2023.

\end{thebibliography}

\end{document}

\texttt{/breakdown} & Lists where your tokens are going, file by file \\
\texttt{/optimize} & Finds low-relevance tabs and suggests closing them \\
\texttt{/pin} & Pins a file so it always stays in context \\
\texttt{/unpin} & Removes the pin from a file \\
\texttt{/model} & Shows which AI model is active or lets you switch \\
\texttt{/preview} & Estimates the token cost of your next message \\
\texttt{/compaction} & Shows how tokens grow with each conversation turn \\
\texttt{/instructions} & Lists instruction files and their token cost \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{VS Code Chat commands available through \texttt{@tokalator}.}
\label{tab:commands}
\end{table}

\subsection{Example: Cleaning Up and Pinning}

Suppose you have 25 tabs open and the budget bar is at 70\%. Type
\texttt{@tokalator /optimize}. Tokalator finds 12 tabs with a relevance score below 0.2
and suggests closing them. After closing, the budget drops to 35\%.

Conversely, if a core file like \texttt{utils.ts} should always be visible to the AI,
type \texttt{@tokalator /pin utils.ts}. The file gets a score of 1.0 and will not be
suggested for removal.


\section{How to Use the MCP Server in Claude Code}

When the MCP server is configured, you can ask Claude Code to use Tokalator tools in
plain English. Claude Code understands the request and calls the right tool for you.

\subsection{Counting Tokens in a File}

Ask Claude Code to count the tokens in any file:

\begin{lstlisting}
> How many tokens are in lib/pricing.ts?

Source:     lib/pricing.ts
Model:      Claude Sonnet 4.5
Tokenizer:  Claude BPE (Anthropic)
Tokens:     3,842
Characters: 14,219
Ratio:      ~3.7 chars/token
\end{lstlisting}

The ratio shows that roughly every 3.7 characters become one token in this file.

\subsection{Checking Your Context Budget}

\begin{lstlisting}
> What is my token budget for lib/pricing.ts,
  components/Calculator.tsx, and app/page.tsx?

Model:    Claude Sonnet 4.5 (200K ctx)
Budget:   18.2K / 200K (9.1%) -- COMFORTABLE

Breakdown:
  Files:          ~12.2K    6.1%
  System prompt:  ~ 2.0K    1.0%
  Instructions:   ~ 0.0K    0.0%
  Conversation:   ~   0K    0.0%
  Output reserve: ~ 4.0K    2.0%
\end{lstlisting}

The three files use 12,200 tokens. Together with the system prompt and output
reservation, that is 9.1\% of the 200,000 token window. The status COMFORTABLE means
there is plenty of room.

\subsection{Previewing a Turn Before Sending}

Before you paste a large block of code into the chat, you can ask Claude Code to preview
how much it would cost:

\begin{lstlisting}
> Preview the token cost if I send this 500-line file

Estimated input:  ~4,200 tokens
Estimated cost:   ~$0.013 (Claude Sonnet 4.5)
Budget after:     22.4K / 200K (11.2%)
\end{lstlisting}

This lets you decide whether to send the full file or just the relevant part.

\subsection{Listing Available Models}

You can ask which models Tokalator knows about. It returns each model with its context
window size and per-million-token prices, helping you compare options before starting a
task.


\section{How Relevance Scoring Works}

When Tokalator assigns a score to an open tab, it checks five signals: (1) whether the
tab shares the same programming language as your active file, (2) whether your active
file imports the tab file, (3) whether they are in the same or nearby folders, (4) how
recently you edited the tab, and (5) whether the tab has compiler errors or warnings.
These signals are combined into a single number between 0 and 1. A score of 0.8 means
the file is very likely useful to the AI. A score of 0.1 means it is probably not needed.
Pinned files and the active editor always get a score of 1.0.


\section{Practical Tips}

\textbf{Close tabs you are not using.} Run \texttt{/optimize} regularly to find
irrelevant tabs. \textbf{Pin files that matter.} Core utility files or type definitions
the AI should always see can be pinned with \texttt{/pin}. \textbf{Watch the budget
after long conversations.} Each turn adds roughly 800 tokens; after 20 turns, that is
16,000 tokens from chat history alone. Use \texttt{/compaction} to check when to start
fresh. \textbf{Choose the right model.} Haiku costs five times less per token than Opus
and handles straightforward tasks well. \textbf{Use caching.} Prompt caching with
Anthropic reduces repeated context cost by up to 90\%.

\section{Availability}

Tokalator is open source (MIT license). The VS Code extension is on the Visual Studio
Marketplace, the MCP server on npm, and the web platform on Vercel.
Source: \url{https://github.com/vfaraji89/tokalator}.


\begin{thebibliography}{9}

\bibitem{bergemann2025}
D.~Bergemann, A.~Bonatti, and A.~Smolin.
\newblock The Economics of Large Language Models.
\newblock \textit{Working Paper}, 2025.

\bibitem{tiktoken}
OpenAI.
\newblock tiktoken: A fast BPE tokeniser for use with OpenAI models.
\newblock \url{https://github.com/openai/tiktoken}, 2023.

\end{thebibliography}

Done. The paper is 4 pages and compiles cleanly. Here is what the new Section 2 ("Why Token Visibility Matters") covers:

- **Context window limits** - when input exceeds the window, context is dropped silently with no warning; monitoring lets developers act before the model loses information
- **Usage and rate limits** - Anthropic and OpenAI impose per-minute and daily token caps that vary by subscription tier (Pro vs Max); hitting the limit stops the service for minutes or hours; a single 80,000-token request can burn a large chunk of the daily allowance
- **Cost accumulation** - input, output, cache write, and cache read tokens each have separate prices; a team of five developers can generate millions of tokens daily without knowing which files or workflows are responsible
- **The core problem** - tokens are invisible by default; editors do not show them and most developers do not check API metadata; Tokalator surfaces this information so developers can close tabs, start fresh conversations, switch models, or use caching

The file is at `paper/demo-paper.tex` and the PDF at `paper/demo-paper.pdf`.

All 87 tests pass across the full project. Here is a summary of the changes:

**Files changed (4):**

1. **`tokalator-extension-vs/src/core/modelProfiles.ts`** - Added `inputCostPerMTok` and `outputCostPerMTok` to `ModelProfile` interface and populated pricing for all 17 models (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google).

3. **`tokalator-extension-vs/src/core/contextMonitor.ts`** - Computes `CostEstimate` in `buildSnapshot()` using the model's per-MTok rates, current input tokens, and max output tokens.

4. **`tokalator-extension-vs/src/webview/contextDashboardProvider.ts`** - New "Estimated Turn Cost" box in the sidebar showing:
   - Total estimated cost (large heading)
   - Input tokens and cost
   - Output tokens (max) and cost
   - Separator with total line
   - Rate line showing $/MTok for input and output
   - Model selector dropdown now shows pricing alongside context window

5. **`tokalator-extension-vs/src/chat/contextChatParticipant.ts`** - Added `fmtCost` helper. `/count` now shows estimated input cost, output cost, and total turn cost. `/model` now shows input and output prices per MTok in the model detail table and in the model list.

file.content:
name: Bi-monthly Wiki Fetch

on:
  schedule:
    # 1st and 15th of every month at 06:00 UTC
    - cron: "0 6 1,15 * *"
  workflow_dispatch: # allow manual trigger

jobs:
  fetch:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: pip install -r scripts/requirements.txt

      - name: Run agentic wiki fetcher
        env:
          GOOGLE_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.GOOGLE_API_KEY }}
          ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
        run: python scripts/fetch-wiki-agent.py

      - name: Commit updated articles
        run: |
          git config user.name "github-actions[bot]"
          git config user.email "github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"
          git add content/wiki/articles.json
          git diff --cached --quiet || git commit -m "chore: wiki fetch $(date +%Y-%m-%d)"
          git push

The workflow runs on a cron schedule (1st and 15th of each month). It has not run recently because:

1. **It only triggers on schedule or manual dispatch.** Since the last commit was pushed today and no manual trigger was fired, it has not run.
2. **GitHub Actions cron schedules only run on the default branch.** If the workflow file is on `main` and the repo is active, it should fire on schedule. But GitHub can silently disable scheduled workflows on repos with no recent activity in 60 days, or if the repo is a fork.

You can trigger it manually right now:

New run is in progress. The problem was:

**`scripts/requirements.txt` had `google-generativeai` (the old SDK) instead of `google-genai` (the newer SDK that `agno` requires).** This caused every scheduled run since at least March 1 to fail with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'google.genai'`.

Fixed by replacing `google-generativeai` with `google-genai`. The fix is now pushed and the workflow has been re-triggered.
